1.  A Claim Petition was preferred under Section 166 and 140 of Motor Vehicle Act on 28.11.2017 for grant of compensation of Rs.25 lakhs by Sh. Avinash Bhadauria (hereinafter called the claimant) against Sh. Bhahampal (hereinafter called the driver/respondent no.1), Sh. Ram Kumar (hereinafter called the owner/respondent no.2) and The National Insurance Company Ltd.
(hereinafter called the insurer/respondent no.3) in respect of injuries sustained by him in an accident which took place on 04.06.2016 at about 08:50 PM on Karnal-Shamli-Meerut Road, near Police Post after Yamuna bridge, toward Uttar Pradesh within the jurisdiction of PS Jhinjhana,
District Shamli, Uttar Pradesh, allegedly caused due to rash and negligent driving of Bajaj Platina Motorcycle bearing Registration no. HR-02U/2017 (hereinafter referred as offending vehicle).
2. It is averred in the petition that on 04.06.2016 at about 08:50 PM, while claimant was crossing the road, he got hit by the offending vehicle, being driven in high speed in a casual and MACT No.
930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.2 of 31 negligent manner. It is also stated therein that two pillion riders were seated on the motor cycle which made it difficult for the driver to control which is why it got rammed into the legs of claimant fracturing his left femur bone. 
It is stated that the police was informed immediately and claimant being injured was rushed to hospital in an ambulance. FIR was registered. The offending vehicle was seized by the police persons and respondent no.1 was arrested. It is also stated that medical bill of sum of Rs.1,32,545/- was reimbursed towards the treatment cost by insurer by the claimant. It is stated that the claimant could not attend to his work for a long time because of the accident. It is stated that responsibility of payment of compensation must be fastened on all the respondents and compensation of Rs.25 lakhs should be awarded in his favour. 
3. Upon receipt of claim petition, notice was directed to be issued to respondents, in response to which counsel for respondent no.1 and 3 appeared. 
4. In the written statement filed on behalf of R1, contradiction has been highlighted in respect to the reason for claimant to cross the road to go the other side after parking his car on one side of the road, as mentioned in the FIR in contrast to what has been stated in the claim petition. It is stated that the offending vehicle was not involved in any accident. Other assertions made in the claim petition were also denied. 
5. No written statement was filed by R2. R2 was proceeded against ex-parte vide order dated 20.05.2019. 
6. Insurance company / R3 did not file any reply. Thus, their MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.3 of 31 right to file the same was closed vide order dated Avinash Bhadauria vs Braham Pal on 1 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10514899/
2 15.07.2019. 
7. An application for assessment of physical disability by Medical Board was filed and allowed, as per which permanent disability has been assessed to be 13% in relation to left lower limb. 
8. From the pleadings of parties, following issues were framed by Ld. Predecessor of this Tribunal vide order dated 15.07.2019 :
i). Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 04.06.2016 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. HR-02U/2017 being driven R1, owned by R2 and insured with R3? OPP.
ii). Whether the petitioner is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP iii). Relief.
9. Thereafter matter was listed for recording of evidence.
10. On 26.02.2024, claimant appeared as PW-1 and tendered his evidentiary affidavit Ex.PW1/1 and also relied upon his proof of official address of the petition I- card, letter of appointment as Ex.PW1/A, certified copy of FIR as Ex.PW1/B, certified copy of charge sheet as Ex.PW1/C, certified copy of Naksha Nazri as Ex.PW1/D, photocopy of RC of offending vehicle as Ex.PW1/E, copy of insurance police as Ex.PW1/F, copy of driving license of R1 as Ex.PW1/G, copy of insurance police of the petitioner as Ex.PW1/H, copy of ITR of the petition as Ex.PW1/J, copy of hospital paper/discharge summary as Ex.PW1/K, original MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs.
Braham Pal & Ors. page no.4 of 31 medical bills as Ex.PW1/L and photocopy of Aadhar card & PAN Card of the petitioner as Ex.PW1/M.
11. No other evidence has been led on behalf of petitioner and PE was closed on 26.02.2024. 
Thereafter, matter was listed for RE, however, RE was not led on behalf of any of the respondents and therefore, RE was closed vide order dated 26.02.2024. 
12. Arguments in detail were addressed by counsels for petitioner, Respondent No.1 as well as Insurance Company. Counsel for claimant has argued that claimant had to suffer on account of irresponsible driving of R1, who was driving the bike without any regard for the applicable traffic rules for which he deserve to compensate him. Counsel for R1 has argued that the accident occurred on account of negligence of claimant who was crossing the road with watermelon in his hand which is why he was not fully conscious while crossing the road. Counsel for R3 argued that the information about the incident was received in the PS after 7 days of the date of accident which shows that the offending vehicle has been implanted further he pointed out that the accident took place on 04.06.2016 as per FIR whereas the date of admission is 05.06.2016. Further, any MLC was not filed. It argued that all the medical bills have already been reimbursed by the insurer of claimant and therefore, he has not suffered any financial loss. Other general defences were also taken. It is Avinash Bhadauria vs Braham Pal on 1 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10514899/
3 prayed that R3 be absolved from any liability towards the claimant. 
13. On the basis of material on record, evidence adduced and MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.5 of 31 arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under :
ISSUE NO.1 "Whether Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 04.06.2016 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. HR-02U/2017 being driven R1, owned by R2 and insured with R3? OPP."
14. What is required to be ascertained is whether rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle was responsible for sustaining injury by injured. 
15. It has been held in catena of cases that negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view is to be taken. It has been further held that the proceedings under the Motor Vehicle Act are not akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence,
strict rules of evidence are not applicable (support drawn from the case of Bimla Devi & Ors. vs.
Himachal Road Transport Corportaion & Ors. [(2009) 13 SCC 530], Kaushnumma Begum and others v/s New India Assurance Company Limited, (2001 ACJ 421 SC), National Insurance Co. Ltd.
vs. Pushpa Rana reported as [2009 ACJ 287].
16. Further, in the present case, police after investigation had filed charge-sheet against respondent no.1 under Section 279 & 338 of IPC which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent no.1 in causing the accident. Including in the case of National Insurance Co. Vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it has been laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India and Hon'ble Delhi High Court that completion of investigation and filing of MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.6 of 31 charge sheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle. 
17. It is also settled that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witness box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him as observed by Hon'ble High Court of India in the case of Cholamandlam insurance company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh, 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310. In the present case also, driver did not enter into the witness box to controvert the claim of petitioner or even to explain circumstances of accident. 
18. PW-1 testified in evidentiary affidavit that he was travelling with his brother in a car passing through Karnal- Shamli-Meeruth Road where he stopped his moving car on one side of the road to relieve himself on the other side of the road. He deposed that it was when he was crossing the road back to return to his car that he was hit by speeding motor cycle, being rashly driven with two pillion riders because of which he sustained serious injury. He was put to elaborate cross examination by counsel for R1 to reflect upon the circumstances of the accident. He explained during cross examination that he stopped vehicle about 200 meter on Karnal-Shamli-Meeruth Road, after crossing Yamuna bridge and then he crossed over the road to go the other side to relieve himself. He admitted that this road was a six lane highway with divider. He declined the suggestion that he Avinash Bhadauria vs Braham Pal on 1 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10514899/
4 crossed the road to purchase watermelon although he admitted that he bought watermelon from the opposite side of the road. He declined the suggestion that he lost his balance while crossing the divider as he was holding watermelon in one hand which is why he fell down on the other MACT No.
930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.7 of 31 side of the road near the divider and sustained injury. He also admitted that there is a police post near the accident although he clarified that he was not aware about it at the time of accident. He also stated that police reached at the spot after a while in his presence followed by an ambulance while his brother verbally complained to the police who advised to get the injury treated first and then complaint be filed. He was also put to cross examination by counsel for R3 but no question was put to him in respect of the mode and manner of accident. 
19. FIR Ex.PW1/C registered on 11.06.2016 upon complaint filed on 10.06.2016 vide General Diary no.021 by Sh. Vikas Singh Bhadhuria brother of Avinash Bhadhuria to the effect that he got injured in an accident on 04.06.2016 at 08:50 PM, for which he was treated at Max Hospital, Vaishali,
Ghaziabad and discharged on 09.06.2016, having been hit by a Bajaj Platina Motor cycle bearing Registration No. HR-02U/2017 on Karnal- Shamli-Meeruth Road in front of police check post. 
20. PW-1 was questioned by counsel for insurance company about the reason as to why the FIR was not immediately lodged to which he responded that his priority was to get himself treated first and then his brother approached the police station to lodge the complaint after his discharge from the hospital. The reason why his brother Sh. Vikas Bhadhoria was a fit person to file complaint with the police was that he was also present at the time of accident along with his brother and even he has been cited as an eye witness in the final charge sheet filed by the police. There is no record filed by claimant to understand whether any police person reached the spot at the accident before he was taken into MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.8 of 31 hospital. 
However reliance can be placed upon the discharge summary of Max Health Care which mentions the history of claimant as having been admitted because of RTA followed by pain swelling and deformity in left thigh, associated with inability to stand and walk. It also mentions the date of admission as 05.06.2016 at 12:54 AM, the time of admission and the reason for admission synchronizes with the affirmation of claimant having met with an accident at about 08:50 PM, on 04.06.2016. The claimant remained admitted and also underwent operative procedure and subsequently discharged on 09.09.2016. On 10.09.2016, complaint was formally filed by the brother of the claimant upon which FIR was registered by the police officials. It is settled that mere delay in filing the FIR does not discredit the claim. Support drawn from the case of Ravi Vs. Badrinarayan and Ors. AIR 2011 Supreme Court 1226 wherein the court observed that lodging the FIR belatedly would not result in dismissal of the claimant. The following observations made in the aforesaid case are pertinent in the context and are reproduced hereunder:
"20. It is well-settled that delay in lodging FIR cannot be a ground to doubt the claimant's case. Knowing the Indian conditions as they are, we cannot expect a common man to first rush to the Police Station immediately after an accident. 
Human nature and family responsibilities occupy the mind of kith and kin to such an extent that they give more importance to get the victim treated rather than to rush to the Police Station. Under such circumstances, they are not expected to act Avinash Bhadauria vs Braham Pal on 1 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10514899/
5 mechanically with promptitude in lodging the FIR with the Police. Delay in lodging the FIR thus, cannot be the ground to deny justice to the victim. In cases of delay, the courts are required to examine the evidence with a closer scrutiny and in MACT No.
930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.9 of 31 doing so; the contents of the FIR should also be scrutinized more carefully. If court finds that there is no indication of fabrication or it has not been concocted or engineered to implicate innocent persons then, even if there is a delay in lodging the FIR, the claim case cannot be dismissed merely on that ground". 
21. "The purpose of lodging the FIR in such type of cases is primarily to intimate the police to initiate investigation of criminal offences. Lodging of FIR certainly proves factum of accident so that the victim is able to lodge a case for compensation but delay in doing so cannot be the main ground for rejecting the claim petition. In other words, although lodging of FIR is vital in deciding motor accident claim cases, delay in lodging the same should not be treated as fatal for such proceedings, if claimant has been able to demonstrate satisfactory and cogent reasons for it. There could be variety of reasons in genuine cases for delayed lodgment of FIR. Unless kith and kin of the victim are able to regain a certain level of tranquility of mind and are composed to lodge it, even if, there is delay, the same deserves to be condoned. In such circumstances, the authenticity of the FIR assumes much more significance than delay in lodging thereof supported by cogent reasons". 
21. In this case, claimant has been able to satisfactory explain the reason for not being able to file the formal complaint immediately after the accident. The accident happened almost in front of the police post. However, there is nothing to ascertain as to whether any police persons was present there. PW-1 stated in his testimony that his brother verbally complained to the police at the spot of accident who also called the ambulance and told them to first get the injuries treated and then file the complaint for lodging the FIR. Nothing has come on record which brings the MACT No.
930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.10 of 31 affirmation of claimant in doubt that he met with an accident as stated in the FIR.
22. As per the circumstances explaining the factual matrix of accident as deposed by PW-1, he had ample time to note down the registration number of offending vehicle as well as to identify the driver thereof. It is not the case that he fell unconscious or that he was all alone or that the offending vehicle merely zipped through the spot of the accident that some credibility can be given to the argument raised on behalf of the insurance company about implanting of offending vehicle to extract the compensation. The details of the offending vehicle were duly mentioned in the FIR. The allegations were investigated into and it was concluded upon investigation that the accident happened because of offending vehicle. In WS filed on behalf of R1, there is a bare denial or involvement of offending vehicle without any explanation of supporting material in reference thereto. Further, during cross examination, such details were put to PW-1 by counsel for R1 which could not have been in knowledge of R1, had he not been present at the spot of accident. There is no alternative explanation led by R1 to show his presence otherwise at the spot of accident. Further, R1 had not stepped into witness box to deny the involvement of the offending vehicle in causing the accident. 
Avinash Bhadauria vs Braham Pal on 1 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10514899/
6 23. PW-1 is the only witness examined. Apart from claimant as PW-1, only R1 could have presented an alternative version explaining the factum of accident. Certain inputs were given duly in cross examination by counsel for R1 to facilitate analysis in respect of alleged negligence of R1 in causing the accident. R1, MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.11 of 31 however, has not led any evidence affirming that accident was not result of his negligent driving of the offending vehicle or that he was following all the traffic rules and regulations and therefore, he was not at fault. There is no categoric denial that he was triple driving at high speed and therefore,
could not exercise sufficient control and ended up ramming into the petitioner when he was crossing the road. It is thus held that the accident in question is attributed casual, irresponsible and reckless driving of offending vehicle by R-1 without having regard to basic traffic norms and regulations and also in utter disregard of safety of fellow commuters. It is also noted that the motorcyclist was triple driving, that too on a highway where average speed of motor vehicle is expected to be 70 kmph to 100 kmph and therefore any rider has to exercise due care and caution while plying thereupon and indulging in street driving could entail serious repercussion for the safety of commuters.
24. Counsel for insurance company has argued that the claimant is guilty of contributory negligence considering that he admitted in cross examination by counsel for R-1 & R-2 that he parked his vehicle on one side of the highway and then crossed over to the other side of the six lane highway in order to relieve himself and then purchased a watermelon from the other side, crossed the divider with watermelon in his hand and it was while crossing the road to get back to his vehicle that accident happened. It is clear that there was no purported designated passage allowing any walker to cross over to other side of the high way. 
25. It is settled that any vehicle should be driven at a speed MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.12 of 31 which enables the driver to stop within limits of his vision and failure to do this would result in the driver being held, partially or fully, responsible for the collision. It is also settled that when an accident happened through combined negligence of two persons, he alone is liable to the other who had the last opportunity of avoiding the accident by reasonable care and who knew or ought to have known the danger caused by the negligence of other person. It is also settled that the crucial question to be answered in case of assessment of contributory negligence is whether either party could by reasonable care, have avoided the consequences of other's negligence. Further, any finding in regard to contributory negligence has to be recorded on the basis of consideration of the pleadings and the evidence adduced and not merely on the basis of police records (support drawn from Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay Vs.
Lakshman Iyer & Ors AIR 2003 SC 4182, Minurout Vs. Satya Pradyumna Mohapatra, (2013)10 SCC 695, Sarla Devi Vs. Royal Sundaram Alliance Insurance Co. Ltd (2014) 15 SCC 450). It is also settled that the burden to prove breach of duty on the part of injured lies on the insurance company and it is obligatory on the part of insurance company to discharge the said burden (Usha Raj Khowa Vs. Paramount Industries (2009) 14 SCC 71). 
26. As such any evidence has not been led by any of the respondent to affirm negligence on the part of claimant/ injured. However, factual circumstances for injured to move across the highway were testified by the claimant himself which can be considered to assess whether petitioner also Avinash Bhadauria vs Braham Pal on 1 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10514899/
7 contributed to the MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.13 of 31 collision. Petitioner is not a local rustic villager of any bordering village, under a compulsion to cross the highway passing through a busy stretch to approach his fields, may be on the other side. He parked the vehicle on one side of the highway at an undesignated place and then opted to cross a six lane highway by jumping over a divider and that too admittedly to relieve himself or to purchase a watermelon. For such frivolous and flimsy reason, he deliberately put his own life and also the life of others plying on the road in peril. Under the circumstance, it cannot be stated that the biker could have solely averted the collision considering that he would not have anticipated any person jumping over the divider to cross over the other side of the road. The pedestrian, under the circumstance was expected to be extra careful and cautious as he was knowingly running the risk of being hit by a speedy vehicle, which injured failed to exercise. Injured is presumably an educated person who would know the applicable traffic rules and is expected to act prudently. Having regard to the discussion made above, it is held that act of petitioner contributed to occurrence of acciden. A contributory negligence to the tune of 25% is held to be attributed to the injured. 
27. As such, in view of the above analysis of material on record, evidence proved on record,
charge-sheet against R-1 and that R-1 did not appear in witness box, he is held to have driven offending motorcycle in a rash and negligent manner with partial negligence also held proved on the part of injured/ petitioner on the scales of preponderance of probabilities. 
28. The issue No.1 is decided accordingly, in favour of the petitioner. 
MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.14 of 31 ii). Whether the petitioner is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom?OPP 29. Section 168 MV Act enjoins the Claim Tribunals to hold an enquiry into the claim to make an effort determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable. Same is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:
"(1) Award of the Claims Tribunal.--On receipt of an application for compensation made under section 166 , the Claims Tribunal shall, after giving notice of the application to the insurer and after giving the parties (including the insurer) an opportunity of being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be,
each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of section 162 may make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and specifying the person or persons to whom compensation shall be paid and in making the award the Claims Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be: Provided that where such application makes a claim for compensation under section 140 in respect of the death or permanent disablement of any person, such claim and any other claim (whether made in such application or otherwise) for compensation in respect of such death or permanent disablement shall Avinash Bhadauria vs Braham Pal on 1 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10514899/
8 be disposed of in accordance with the provisions of Chapter X. (2) The Claims Tribunal shall arrange to deliver copies of the award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award. (3) When an award is made under this section, the person who is required to pay any amount in terms MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal &
Ors. page no.15 of 31 of such award shall, within thirty days of the date of announcing the award by the Claims Tribunal, deposit the entire amount awarded in such manner as the Claims Tribunal may direct." 
30. Before putting in frame the position of law, it is noted that the process of determining the compensation by the court is essentially a very difficult task and can never be an exact science. 
Perfect compensation is hardly possible, more so in claims of injury and disability. (As observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Sidram Vs. The Divisional Manager United India Insurance Company Ltd, SLP (Civil) No. 19277 of 2019). 
31 The basic principle in assessing motor vehicle compensation claims, is to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in before the accident, with other compensatory directions for loss of amenities and other payments. These general principles have been stated and reiterated in several decisions. [Support drawn from Govind Yadav v. New India Insurance Co. Ltd., (2011) 10 SCC 683] . 
32. This Tribunal has been tasked with determination of just compensation. The observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Divisional Controller, KSRTC v. Mahadeva Shetty and Another,
(2003) 7 SCC 197, needs mention here (para 15): 
"Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but the same should not be a pittance. The courts and tribunals have a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of compensation, which should be just. What would be "just"
compensation is a vexed question. There can be no golden rule applicable to all cases for measuring MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.16 of 31 the value of human life or a limb. Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise mathematical calculations. It would depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special features, if any. Every method or mode adopted for assessing compensation has to be considered in the background of "just" compensation which is the pivotal consideration. Though by use of the expression "which appears to it to be just", a wide discretion is vested in the Tribunal, the determination has to be rational, to be done by a judicious approach and not the outcome of whims,
wild guesses and arbitrariness.. ..." 
33. Delineating the damages as pecuniary and non pecuniary, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in case of R. D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control ( India) Pvt Ltd, 1995 AIR 755, made following observations:

9 "9....while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages. 
Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non- pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations. In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial;
(iii) other material loss. So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future;
(ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.17 of 31 not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, hardship,
discomfort, disappointment, frustration and mental stress in life." 
34. Certain principles for delineating just compensation were enumerated in the case of Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343, by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India. Following observations are relevant in the context:
"40.General principles relating to compensation in injury cases 5. The provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident. The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. 
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. [See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 :
1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 : (1970) 2 WLR MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.18 of 31 50 : (1969)
3 All ER 1528 (HL)] . ]
6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:

10 Pecuniary damages (Special damages) 
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii)(a) and (iv).
It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii), (v)
and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses,
loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
7. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii)(a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence. 
Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item MACT No. 930/2017 Avinash Bhadauriya Vs. Braham Pal & Ors. page no.19 of 31 (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof.

having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.
Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit and to release even the whole amount in the case Avinash Bhadauria vs Braham Pal on 1 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10514899/
16 of literate persons.
They are taking such a rigid and mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semi literate and literate persons.
The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money.

The guidelines cast a responsibility on the Tribunals to pass appropriate orders after examining each case on its own merits.
investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit is directed by the Tribunals as a matter of course and in a routine manner, ignoring the object and the spirit of the guidelines issued by this Court and the genuine requirements of the claimants.
